questions.explain: The first pair of digits identifies the western grid line and the second identifies the southern grid line. Together they locate the 1 km square extending northeast from that southwest corner.

choices: The same as latitude and longitude
A flat kilometre grid over Great Britain
A grid used only at sea
questions.explain: The British National Grid projects positions onto a flat coordinate system expressed in metres. It supports grid distances and references, while latitude and longitude describe angular position on Earth.

why: A grid reference locates a square using eastings followed by northings. More digits identify a smaller square, while the two-letter code identifies the 100 km square it lies in.

The easting measures how far east of the square’s western edge you are, and the northing how far north of its southern edge, so you go along before you go up. Each extra pair of figures divides the square by ten: within a 100 km square, two figures give a 10 km square, four give 1 km and six give 100 m. The same numbers repeat in every 100 km square, so the letter pair (such as SH) is needed to say which one.
The map is fictional, and a more precise reference does not by itself make a measurement more accurate.

glossary.def: A grid coordinate measuring distance east from a defined origin. Read eastings before northings in a grid reference.

A map-grid coordinate measuring distance north from the grid’s defined origin. Read it after the easting when giving a grid reference. The coordinate locates a position within a projected grid; it is not the same quantity as latitude.

A reference identifying a 1 km square on a standard British National Grid map by its southwest corner. Read the easting first and then the northing. It identifies a square, not an exact point within it.

A reference locating a 100 m square within a standard British National Grid kilometre square. Read three easting figures before three northing figures. Adding figures improves reference precision, but the map and observation still limit accuracy.
Ordnance Survey Great Britain. OSGB36 is a geodetic datum used with the British National Grid; it differs from the global WGS84 reference system.
An offset origin used to keep map-grid coordinates convenient and usually positive. The British National Grid uses one southwest of Great Britain.
An area identified by a map grid. In British National Grid notation, four, six and eight figures identify 1 km, 100 m and 10 m squares respectively.
A global geodetic reference system used by GPS, including a reference ellipsoid and coordinate frame. Converting to the British National Grid requires a projection and datum transformation.

misconception.claim: A six-figure British National Grid reference identifies an exact point.
misconception.truth: A six-figure reference identifies a 100-metre square within the relevant lettered grid square. More digits specify a smaller area, but extra precision does not guarantee an accurate observation. Read eastings before northings and include the letter pair when the wider location is needed.

misconceptions.claim: A six-figure British National Grid reference identifies an exact point.
misconceptions.truth: A six-figure reference identifies a 100-metre square within the relevant lettered grid square. More digits specify a smaller area, but extra precision does not guarantee an accurate observation. Read eastings before northings and include the letter pair when the wider location is needed.

Set Easting, then Northing, and read the six-figure reference. Then explain how adding the two-letter code (such as SH) identifies which 100 km square it lies in.
pitfalls: Read eastings before northings and distinguish the projected grid from latitude and longitude.
Explain that a six-figure reference identifies a 100 m square rather than an exact point within it.
Check the coordinate system before comparing an OS grid reference with a GPS location.

modelNotes: A complete short reference needs the 100 km letter pair followed by eastings and northings.
Six figures identify a 100 m square, not a surveyed point accurate to one metre.
Four figures such as 1234 identify the 1 km square with southwest corner at easting 12 and northing 34.
Six figures subdivide to 100 m, and eight figures to 10 m.
This fictional map covers one 100 km square; its main grid lines are 10 km apart.

labs.title: Mass movement
labs.hook: Gravity drives a slope downhill while friction and cohesion resist movement.
labs.objective: Identify the main parts of a rotational slump and explain how rainfall can reduce the stability of a slope.
curriculum: AQA GCSE 3.1.3.2 Coastal landscapes in the UK
AQA A-level 3.1.3 Coastal systems and landscapes
Edexcel GCSE A Topic 1 Changing landscapes of the UK
Edexcel GCSE B Topic 4 UK’s evolving physical landscape
OCR GCSE A Landscapes of the UK

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the crown, the curved shear surface and the toe. Read the starting factor of safety, then open How to read these results for the soil strength values.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Pore pressure and explain why resistance falls as effective stress drops. Once the factor of safety is below 1, press Play to watch the slump rotate.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does increasing pore pressure reduce the resistance to sliding along the selected surface?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: A rotational slump moves along a curved slip surface, so the displaced block rotates as it descends. The head drops and may tilt backwards while material moves outward near the toe.

questions.prompt: Rain makes till more likely to fail because…
choices: It freezes and wedges the cliff apart
It cements the clay particles together
questions.explain: Higher pore-water pressure reduces the effective stress pressing soil particles together. This weakens frictional resistance and can make a slope more likely to fail.

questions.prompt: When pore pressure pushes the factor of safety below 1, Play shows…
choices: The slope stays as it is
The head drops and the toe moves outward
The toe drops and the head moves outward
The whole slope slides as one flat sheet
questions.explain: A factor of safety below 1 means the forces driving movement exceed those resisting it. The rotation shown illustrates that unstable state; it does not predict how fast or how far a real slide moves.

questions.prompt: Before comparing a real coastal slide with this model, check…
choices: Whether both slopes face the sea
Whether the cliffs are equally high
Its material, pore pressure and slip shape
How much rain fell that year
questions.explain: Material strength, pore pressure and the geometry of the failure surface determine whether a rotational mechanism is plausible. Two coastal slopes can fail differently despite sharing a similar setting.

why: Gravity drives a slope downhill while friction and cohesion resist movement. Rising pore-water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance, making a chosen slip surface less stable.

Water in the pores pushes soil grains apart, so less of the soil's weight presses the grains together along the slip surface. Friction depends on that effective stress, so resistance falls while the driving weight stays almost the same; when resistance drops below the driving force, the factor of safety falls below 1.
The factor of safety applies to the starting slope and its chosen slip surface; the rotation that follows is illustrative, not a calculated runout.

glossary.def: A landslide in which a mass of soil or rock rotates along a curved slip surface. The upper part commonly drops and tilts back, while material moves outward near the toe. Water pressure can reduce the slope’s resistance to failure.

A surface along which adjacent masses move relative to each other. In a landslide it separates moving material from the underlying slope and may be curved or nearly planar. It is distinct from the exposed cliff or landslide scar.

The upper edge of a landslide, where displaced material separates from stable ground. Cracks near the crown can outline the developing failure. It is distinct from the toe, where displaced material accumulates farther down the slope.
The downslope end of a landslide or other mass-movement deposit. Displaced material may thicken or bulge there as it slows. It differs from the crown, where material separates from the stable slope.
The pressure of water or gas within pores in soil or rock. Increasing water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance to slope failure.

Unsorted sediment deposited directly by glacier ice, often containing a mixture from clay to boulders. Its poor sorting distinguishes it from many meltwater deposits reworked by flowing water. Till can form several types of glacial landform.

The downslope movement of rock or soil under gravity, including falls, slides and flows. Water can increase weight or pore pressure and may be mixed with the moving material. Gravity provides the driving force rather than a transporting river or wind.

misconception.claim: Rain can destabilise a slope only by making the material heavier.
misconception.truth: Added water can increase weight, but rising pore-water pressure can also reduce effective stress and frictional resistance along a potential slip surface. Drainage, cohesion, slope geometry and material properties influence stability, so the effect is not explained by added mass alone.

misconceptions.claim: Rain can destabilise a slope only by making the material heavier.
misconceptions.truth: Added water can increase weight, but rising pore-water pressure can also reduce effective stress and frictional resistance along a potential slip surface. Drainage, cohesion, slope geometry and material properties influence stability, so the effect is not explained by added mass alone.

teacher.script:
Find the crown, the curved shear surface and the toe. Read the starting factor of safety, then open How to read these results for the soil strength values.

Increase Pore pressure and explain why resistance falls as effective stress drops. Once the factor of safety is below 1, press Play to watch the slump rotate.
pitfalls: Consider slope material, gravity and water pressure together rather than attributing every failure to wave erosion.
Distinguish a rockfall from a slide or flow by describing how the material moves.
Explain how saturation can reduce slope stability, including on slopes that are not beside the sea.

modelNotes: A simplified Bishop calculation divides the initial sliding mass into 160 vertical slices.
Effective cohesion is 2 kPa, friction angle 15°, and soil unit weight 20 kN/m³.

labs.title: Rain shadow
labs.hook: Rising air expands and cools.
labs.objective: Explain why rising air cools and produces rain on a windward slope, leaving drier conditions on the leeward side.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Predict which side the air rises and cools on. Set Initial humidity to 20% and Ridge height to 900 m: why does no cloud form?

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Initial humidity to 70% and Ridge height to 2100 m, and follow the parcel through cloud base. Compare the temperatures at the windward and leeward feet and explain the difference.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can air arrive at the leeward foot of a mountain warmer and drier than when it began rising?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Air rising on the windward slope…
questions.explain: Rising air encounters lower pressure, expands and cools. If it cools to saturation, water vapour can condense into cloud droplets.

choices: On the leeward side of the barrier
questions.explain: Air crossing a mountain can lose moisture on the windward side and then warm as it descends downwind. The resulting lower relative humidity helps create a drier leeward region.

questions.prompt: If the ridge is higher than the parcel’s condensation level…
choices: Cloud forms; the leeward air arrives warmer and drier
The leeward air arrives colder and wetter
No cloud forms on either side
questions.explain: Above its condensation level, the parcel cools more slowly because condensation releases latent heat. Once the moisture has rained out, it descends at the faster dry rate, so it reaches the same height warmer and drier. The model does not calculate rainfall totals.

questions.prompt: Why are Owens Valley (east of the Sierra Nevada) and Penrith (east of the Lake District) both relatively dry?
choices: They are both far inland from the sea
Cold valley air stops clouds forming
Air loses rain over hills upwind, then sinks
Both lie under subtropical high pressure
questions.explain: Both examples involve moist air rising over a barrier and descending on its sheltered side. Their rainfall contrasts also depend on prevailing winds, moisture supply and the wider regional climate.

why: Rising air expands and cools. If it reaches saturation, condensation can occur; after moisture is lost, descent on the far side of a ridge can bring warmer, drier air to the same elevation.

Below cloud base the rising air cools at the dry rate, about 9.8 °C per kilometre. Above it, condensation releases latent heat, so the saturated air cools more slowly (6 °C/km in this model). Once that water has fallen as rain, the sinking air warms at the faster dry rate all the way down, so it reaches the leeward foot warmer and with lower relative humidity than when it started.
The parcel uses fixed lapse rates and assumes all condensed water rains out; it compares temperatures but does not calculate rainfall.

glossary.def: Precipitation associated with air being lifted over high ground. Rising air expands and cools; if it becomes saturated, cloud can form and precipitation may follow. The lee side may receive less rain, depending on the wider weather pattern.

A relatively dry area on the sheltered side of high ground. Uplift and precipitation can remove moisture from approaching air, while descending air warms and its relative humidity falls. Prevailing winds influence the strength of the effect.

The side of a feature that faces the approaching wind. Moist air forced upward there may form cloud and rain. Windward is relative to wind direction, so it does not always mean the same compass-facing slope.
The side sheltered from the prevailing wind. Descending air there often warms and has lower relative humidity.
Cooling as an air parcel expands when pressure falls, without exchanging heat with its surroundings. Rising air commonly cools this way.

A warm, often dry wind descending on the sheltered side of a mountain range. Air warms as it is compressed during descent, and moisture loss or differences in source air can intensify the effect. Föhn and chinook are regional names.
In a rain-shadow model, high ground that forces approaching air to rise; its height and orientation influence uplift.

misconception.claim: A mountain creates the moisture that falls as rain on its windward side.
misconception.truth: The approaching air already carries water vapour. Forced uplift makes it expand and cool; if it becomes saturated, cloud and rain can form. Having lost moisture, the air warms as it descends, so the leeward side is often warmer and drier.

misconceptions.claim: A mountain creates the moisture that falls as rain on its windward side.
misconceptions.truth: The approaching air already carries water vapour. Forced uplift makes it expand and cool; if it becomes saturated, cloud and rain can form. Having lost moisture, the air warms as it descends, so the leeward side is often warmer and drier.

teacher.script:
Predict which side the air rises and cools on. Set Initial humidity to 20% and Ridge height to 900 m: why does no cloud form?

Set Initial humidity to 70% and Ridge height to 2100 m, and follow the parcel through cloud base. Compare the temperatures at the windward and leeward feet and explain the difference.
pitfalls: Explain that uplift can cool moist air to condensation; a mountain does not create the water vapour.
Distinguish local windward and leeward contrasts from broad climate patterns associated with latitude.
Use long-term climate evidence before classifying a relatively dry valley as a desert.

modelNotes: Unsaturated air cools at about 9.8 °C per kilometre as it rises.
Above cloud base, the model uses a fixed saturated lapse rate of 6 °C/km; real values vary with temperature and pressure.

Relief is drawn 2.5 times taller than true; Physical scale uses the same scale in every direction. Ground colour and trees are schematic: the lee side is drawn drier only in proportion to the water the air loses on the way up.

labs.title: Groundwater
labs.hook: Groundwater fills connected pores and fractures below the water table.
labs.objective: Locate water in connected pores and explain how pumping changes the water table and flow towards a well.
curriculum: AQA A-level 3.1.1 Water and carbon cycles

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Before pumping, find the saturated pores and the water table. Raise Pump and compare the well head with the Boundary head.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn on Confined aquifer. Explain why the gold Potentiometric surface sits above the clay layer, and why it shows the level water would rise to in a well, not a lake.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does lowering the water level in a well change the hydraulic gradient around it?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: The top of the saturated zone in the pores
An underground lake with a shore
A river flowing under the ground
The boundary between soil and bedrock
questions.explain: The water table is the upper surface of the saturated zone in an unconfined aquifer. Beneath it, connected pores and fractures are filled with water rather than air.

choices: Rock that stores and yields useful water
Rock that water cannot pass through
questions.explain: An aquifer must both store groundwater and transmit it readily enough to supply useful quantities. High water content alone is insufficient if pore connections or fractures do not allow water to flow.

questions.prompt: In this steady unconfined model, increasing pumping makes the nearby water table…
choices: Stay level because the boundary refills it
Lower into a cone of depression
Fall evenly across the whole aquifer
questions.explain: Pumping lowers hydraulic head near the well, creating a gradient that draws groundwater towards it. This steady model balances that inflow against pumping and does not track long-term exhaustion of a finite store.

questions.prompt: In the confined model, pumping lowers the gold surface. What happens to the sand beneath the clay layer?
choices: It drains and fills with air near the well
It turns into an empty cone below the well
It refills at once, so its pressure is unchanged
It stays saturated while the water pressure falls
questions.explain: A confined aquifer stays fully saturated under its aquitard. Pumping lowers the pressure, so the potentiometric surface (the level water would rise to in a well) falls, but the pores remain full of water.

why: Groundwater fills connected pores and fractures below the water table. Pumping lowers hydraulic head near a well, creating a gradient that draws water towards it.

In a confined aquifer the sand stays fully saturated beneath the clay aquitard, so pumping does not drain the pores. Instead it lowers the water pressure, and the potentiometric surface (the level water would rise to in a well) falls into a cone around the well.
The steady-flow calculation holds the outer head fixed; it does not determine recharge, long-term depletion or sustainable abstraction.

glossary.def: The upper surface of an unconfined groundwater body, below which connected pores are saturated. Its height changes with recharge and groundwater flow. In a confined aquifer, the level reached in a well represents pressure head rather than a free water table.

A body of permeable rock or sediment that stores groundwater and allows useful amounts to flow through it. Water occupies connected pores or fractures; an aquifer is usually not an underground lake. Both storage space and connectivity matter.
A layer of rock or sediment with low permeability that slows groundwater flow. It may confine an aquifer without being completely impermeable.

A lowering of the water table or groundwater pressure surface around a pumping well. Water flows towards the well down this hydraulic gradient. The cone is a pattern in water levels, not an empty cone excavated in the rock.

The addition of water to an aquifer, usually as infiltrated rainfall or surface water percolates downwards. Recharge may take time and vary strongly by season and geology. It is not identical to all rainfall falling on the land above.

A line of springs where groundwater emerges along a geological or topographic boundary, often where permeable rock meets less permeable material. Its position reflects underground flow paths and can help explain the location of settlements.
A saturated permeable layer bounded above by a low-permeability layer. Water in a well rises to its pressure level, which may or may not reach the ground surface.

misconception.claim: Groundwater usually occupies a single underground lake.
misconception.truth: Most groundwater occupies connected pores and fractures in rock or sediment. In an unconfined aquifer, the water table marks the top of the saturated zone. In a confined aquifer, water in a well may rise above the aquifer because of pressure rather than an underground open lake.

misconceptions.claim: Groundwater usually occupies a single underground lake.
misconceptions.truth: Most groundwater occupies connected pores and fractures in rock or sediment. In an unconfined aquifer, the water table marks the top of the saturated zone. In a confined aquifer, water in a well may rise above the aquifer because of pressure rather than an underground open lake.

cases.label: Dust Bowl and the Ogallala aquifer

teacher.script:
Before pumping, find the saturated pores and the water table. Raise Pump and compare the well head with the Boundary head: the difference is the drawdown shown in the readout.

Turn on Confined aquifer. The gold potentiometric surface is the level water would rise to in a well; the aquifer below the clay stays saturated even when that level falls.
pitfalls: Show groundwater occupying pores and fractures rather than presenting underground rivers as the usual arrangement.
Explain that pumping removes water from an existing store and can lower the water table.
Distinguish a rock’s ability to store water from its ability to transmit enough water to act as a useful aquifer.

modelNotes: Hydraulic conductivity is 10 m/day, well radius 0.2 m, outer radius 500 m and confined thickness 12 m.

labs.title: Isostasy
labs.hook: Adding an ice load changes the equilibrium height of the crust.
labs.objective: Explain how the crust responds to loading and unloading, using an ice sheet to explore subsidence and rebound.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the crust, the Moho and the solid mantle. Set Ice thickness to 0 m, predict which way the crust will move, then set it to 3000 m.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Calculate 3000 × 917/3300 and compare it with the depression shown in the readout. Switch to Physical scale to remove the ×5 vertical exaggeration; the width of the ice sheet stays schematic.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why adding an ice load depresses the crust and why removing it allows rebound.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: The crust is fixed to the core
The crust floats in balance on the mantle
Plates move only at their edges
Mountains stay up because rock is strong
questions.explain: Isostasy describes the tendency towards gravitational balance between lithospheric loads and the material beneath them. The mantle is mostly solid but can deform and flow over geological timescales.

questions.prompt: After an ice sheet melts, the land…
questions.explain: Removing an ice sheet reduces the load on the lithosphere, allowing uplift as the underlying mantle readjusts. This response can continue for thousands of years after the ice has melted.

questions.prompt: If you increase Ice thickness, the crustal block should…
choices: Tilt but keep its average height
questions.explain: Adding ice increases the weight supported by the underlying material. In this local balance model, the crustal block sinks farther to displace enough denser mantle to support the added load.

questions.prompt: What process links raised beaches in western Scotland with the rising shore of Hudson Bay?
choices: Both lost ice and are still rebounding
Both sit on a rising hotspot
Both are folding as plates collide
questions.explain: Both regions carried thick ice sheets whose removal initiated ongoing crustal uplift. Raised shorelines record the resulting change in land level relative to the sea, together with any sea-level changes.

why: Adding an ice load changes the equilibrium height of the crust. In the local Airy model, a denser mantle supports a less dense crustal column, and unloading raises its equilibrium position.

At equilibrium every column must have the same mass above a deep compensation level. Ice adds mass, so the column sinks until it has pushed aside an equal mass of mantle: 1 m of ice (917 kg/m³) displaces about 0.28 m of mantle (3300 kg/m³). Because ice is far less dense than mantle rock, even 3000 m of ice lowers the land by only about 830 m.
The experiment calculates an equilibrium displacement; actual rebound takes time as the solid mantle deforms.

glossary.def: The gravitational balance in which the lithosphere is supported by denser material beneath it. Adding or removing a large load causes deformation and adjustment over time. The mantle flows slowly as solid rock rather than as a simple liquid ocean.

The gradual rise of land following the removal of a large ice load. The solid Earth adjusts as mantle material flows slowly over time. Rebound changes relative sea level locally, even while global mean sea level may rise.
A former beach now above present sea level because of land uplift, a fall in sea level, or both.

Earth’s rigid outer mechanical layer, comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle. It is divided into tectonic plates and overlies the weaker asthenosphere. The lithosphere is therefore thicker than the crust alone.
A mechanically weak part of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere. It is predominantly solid rock that deforms slowly over geological time.

In isostasy, the thickened lower part of continental crust beneath a mountain belt. Less dense crust extends deeper into the mantle and helps support high topography. The term describes crustal structure, not a literal plant-like shape.
Describing a change in global mean sea level, for example from changing ocean-water volume or ocean-basin capacity.

misconception.claim: Postglacial rebound shows that the mantle beneath the crust is liquid lava.
misconception.truth: The mantle is mostly solid rock that can deform slowly over long timescales. When an ice load is removed, the land rises towards a new balance as mantle rock slowly flows back. This lab calculates the final balance, not how fast rebound happens.

misconceptions.claim: Postglacial rebound shows that the mantle beneath the crust is liquid lava.
misconceptions.truth: The mantle is mostly solid rock that can deform slowly over long timescales. When an ice load is removed, the land rises towards a new balance as mantle rock slowly flows back. This lab calculates the final balance, not how fast rebound happens.

teacher.script:
Identify the crust, the Moho and the solid mantle. Set Ice thickness to 0 m, predict which way the crust will move, then set it to 3000 m.

Calculate 3000 × 917/3300 and compare it with the depression shown in the readout. Switch to Physical scale to remove the ×5 vertical exaggeration; the width of the ice sheet stays schematic.
pitfalls: Explain how the lithosphere responds to loading rather than treating the crust as resting on a rigid floor.
Describe the mantle as predominantly solid material that can flow slowly over long timescales.
Distinguish local changes in relative sea level caused by rebound from changes in global sea level.

modelNotes: This local Airy experiment keeps a 35 km crustal column unchanged and adds up to 3000 m of ice.
Crust, mantle and ice densities are 2800, 3300 and 917 kg/m³.
Equal mass above a compensation depth gives an equilibrium depression of ice thickness × 917/3300.

labs.title: Wilson cycle
labs.hook: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while subduction can later consume oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together.
labs.objective: Follow the opening and closing of an ocean basin and relate continental collision to the formation of mountain belts.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Continental rift, then Young ocean and Open ocean. Find the ridge and the thin oceanic crust.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to Subduction begins and follow the slab. Compare Ocean closes with Continental collision and find the mountain root.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does subduction turn an expanding ocean into a closing basin?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Oceans opening and closing over geological time
The yearly cycle of ocean currents
Continents drifting in one direction forever
The cycle of rock types forming
questions.explain: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while later subduction can consume its oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together again. The Wilson cycle summarises these possible stages over geological time.

choices: An older ocean that opened and then closed
A rift that never became an ocean
A transform fault like San Andreas
questions.explain: Parts of the Caledonian and Appalachian mountain belts preserve evidence of convergence and collisions associated with closure of the Iapetus Ocean. Later Atlantic opening separated sections of that older mountain system.

questions.prompt: If you move Formation stage towards Continental collision, the ocean should…
questions.explain: As subduction consumes oceanic lithosphere, the basin narrows and the bordering continents approach one another. Continental collision then shortens and thickens crust, producing a mountain belt.

questions.prompt: Iceland, on today’s Mid-Atlantic Ridge, shows which stage?
questions.explain: Iceland lies on the active Mid-Atlantic spreading ridge, where plates separate and new oceanic crust forms. It therefore represents ongoing ocean-basin opening rather than closure by continental collision.

why: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while subduction can later consume oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together. Mountain belts can preserve evidence of oceans that have closed.

Old oceanic lithosphere is cold and dense, so it can sink beneath a continent at a trench. Once subduction consumes plate faster than the ridge makes it, the basin narrows. Continental crust is too buoyant to sink far, so when the continents meet the crust crumples and thickens into a mountain belt with a deep root.
The six stages organise possible tectonic changes; they are not a fixed schedule followed by every ocean basin.

glossary.def: A framework describing the opening and eventual closing of an ocean basin through rifting, seafloor spreading, subduction and continental collision. Different basins follow different histories. Geological structures can preserve evidence of stages even after an ocean has disappeared.
An elongated region where the lithosphere is extending and thinning. Some continental rifts develop into ocean basins; others stop before an ocean forms.

A transition between continental and oceanic crust that is not an active plate boundary. Many Atlantic margins developed after continental rifting. Sediment accumulation, subsidence and occasional earthquakes can still occur, so passive does not mean completely inactive.

A period or process of mountain building involving deformation and thickening of the crust. Plate collision and subduction are common settings. Mountains may later be eroded, leaving folded rocks and other evidence of an older mountain belt.
An ancient mountain belt formed during Palaeozoic continental collisions, now exposed in places including Scotland, Scandinavia and Greenland.
An ancient mountain belt in eastern North America, assembled through several Palaeozoic collisions during the closing of oceans and formation of Pangaea.
A body of crust with a geological history distinct from neighbouring regions, often joined to a continent by tectonic accretion.

misconception.claim: Every ocean basin follows the same fixed timetable from opening to closure.
misconception.truth: The Wilson cycle organises possible stages of rifting, ocean spreading, subduction and collision. Real basins differ in geometry, plate motions and duration, and some rifts stop developing. The framework helps interpret geological evidence without prescribing one schedule for every ocean.

misconceptions.claim: Every ocean basin follows the same fixed timetable from opening to closure.
misconceptions.truth: The Wilson cycle organises possible stages of rifting, ocean spreading, subduction and collision. Real basins differ in geometry, plate motions and duration, and some rifts stop developing. The framework helps interpret geological evidence without prescribing one schedule for every ocean.

teacher.script:
Choose Continental rift, then Young ocean and Open ocean. Find the ridge and the thin oceanic crust.

Switch to Subduction begins and follow the slab. Compare Ocean closes with Continental collision and find the mountain root.
pitfalls: Use Pangaea as one example within a longer history of continental assembly and breakup.
Place Iceland at a divergent boundary rather than using it as an example of continental collision.
Connect the closing of an ocean with later mountain building while allowing for more complex histories in real regions.

modelNotes: The unstretched reference continent is 35 km thick and the oceanic crust about 7 km thick; both overlie solid mantle. Collision thickens the crust to about 65 km beneath peaks about 5–6 km high. Lithosphere and slab thicknesses are simplified to fit the section.
Physical scale removes the ×2 vertical exaggeration. The 300 km section shows only part of a basin.

labs.title: Soil catena
labs.hook: Soils along a slope are linked by movement of water and sediment.
labs.objective: Compare soil profiles from the crest to the foot of a slope and explain how water and sediment movement connect them.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate the crest, backslope and toe, which share one parent material. Read the three soil thicknesses.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Slope and watch the backslope soil thin while the toe soil thickens. Use Compare physical scale to tell soil thickness apart from the height of the slope.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How can movement of water and sediment connect soil differences along a single slope?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: The same soil across a whole region
A sequence of linked soils down one slope
questions.explain: A catena links soils along a slope where drainage and the transfer of material vary with topographic position. These differences can produce distinct profiles even where the parent material is similar.

questions.prompt: Why may an upper-slope soil be thinner than the toe soil?
choices: Soil moves downslope and collects below
It has been forming for longer
More rain falls on the upper slope
questions.explain: Erosion can remove material from upper slopes while deposition adds it near the foot of a slope. The resulting thickness pattern also depends on soil formation, drainage and local conditions.

questions.prompt: In this model, steepening the slope makes the backslope soil…
questions.explain: The model is set up so that the backslope soil thins as the slope steepens. This shows a likely relationship; it does not calculate an erosion rate.

questions.prompt: A Yorkshire valley side and an Iowa loess hill are paired in this lab because…
choices: Both show soils changing down a slope
questions.explain: Both examples compare soils at different positions along a slope rather than assuming a whole region has one profile. Keeping parent material similar helps reveal the effects of drainage and downslope transport.

why: Soils along a slope are linked by movement of water and sediment. Upper slopes may lose material while lower slopes receive it, creating differences even where parent material is similar.

On the steeper backslope, soil creep, rainsplash and surface wash move soil downslope faster than weathering can replace it, so the soil stays thin. At the toe this colluvium builds up, and water draining from upslope keeps the subsoil saturated for long periods, so it becomes grey and mottled (gleyed).
The selected thickness pattern is one example; climate, drainage and land use can produce a different catena.

glossary.def: A sequence of soils along a slope whose differences are related to relief, drainage and movement of sediment. Compare a freely drained crest with a wetter footslope. A catena need not form a perfectly regular sequence in every landscape.
The highest part of a hill or ridge. Soil thickness and drainage there depend on the local relief, geology and climate.
The main, usually steep section of a hillslope between its shoulder and footslope; material commonly moves through it downslope.
The lowest part of a hillslope, where it meets the valley floor. Water and sediment from upslope collect here, so soils are often thicker and wetter.
Soil features associated with prolonged saturation and oxygen shortage, often including grey colours and rusty mottles from changes in iron chemistry.
A traditional soil term for a shallow, often acidic soil over hard, non-calcareous rock; commonly found on steep or exposed ground.

Loose sediment accumulated on or near the foot of a slope through gravity-driven movement and surface wash. It commonly contains a mixture of particle sizes. Unlike alluvium, it is not defined by deposition from a river channel.

misconception.claim: Soils on one hillside must be identical because they share a climate.
misconception.truth: Position on a slope affects drainage, erosion, deposition and the movement of dissolved material. These differences can produce contrasting soils even on similar parent material under the same regional climate. The pattern depends on local conditions rather than a universal sequence of thicknesses.

Locate the crest, backslope and toe, which share one parent material. Read the three soil thicknesses.

Increase Slope and watch the backslope soil thin while the toe soil thickens. Use Compare physical scale to tell soil thickness apart from the height of the slope.
pitfalls: Consider slope position, drainage and material movement alongside climate when comparing soils along a hillslope.
Use evidence of erosion and accumulation rather than assuming that the thickest soil must occur at the crest.
Distinguish a catena’s sequence of soil profiles from a texture triangle that classifies mineral particle proportions.

labs.title: Periglacial landforms
labs.hook: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years.
labs.objective: Explain how repeated freezing and thawing produce ice wedges and patterned ground in cold landscapes.
curriculum: AQA A-level 3.1.4 Glacial systems and landscapes

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Define permafrost and explain how ground ice differs from a glacier. Play one year and watch the active layer thaw down to the dashed line.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Wedge development and trace the tapering wedge of ice. Explain how winter cracking, meltwater and refreezing make it grow, then set View to Polygon network.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how repeated thermal cracking and refreezing build an ice wedge over many years.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: Periglacial environments are dominated by cold-ground processes such as seasonal freezing and, in some settings, permafrost. They do not require a glacier to occupy the site.

choices: Frozen cracks refill with ice each year
questions.explain: Strong winter cooling can crack frozen ground, and meltwater entering the cracks can freeze. Repeated cracking and ice addition over many years can build a wedge of ground ice.

questions.prompt: What does Wedge development change here?
choices: A set wedge width, with no rate
questions.explain: Wedge development sets the wedge width so that different stages of growth can be compared. It does not assign a growth rate or a number of years.

questions.prompt: Cairngorm blockfields and Alaskan ice-wedge polygons are grouped together because…
choices: Both are linked to cold ground, not glacier ice
Both were carved by valley glaciers
Both formed under thick ice sheets
Both are active only in summer
questions.explain: Blockfields and ice-wedge polygons illustrate different processes associated with cold ground. Neither requires the local landscape to have been carved by an actively flowing valley glacier.

why: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. Seasonal thaw affects its active layer, while repeated thermal cracking and refreezing can build ice wedges.
Increase Wedge development and trace the tapering wedge of ice. Explain how winter cracking, meltwater and refreezing make it grow, then set View to Polygon network.
The annual cycle and accumulated wedge width are separate comparisons; the width slider does not specify a growth rate.

glossary.def: Describing processes and landforms associated with cold ground, including freeze–thaw, frost sorting and thermal cracking. They may occur near glaciers or far from present ice. Relict features can remain after a region’s climate has become warmer.
A wedge of ground ice formed as water enters thermal-contraction cracks and freezes repeatedly in permafrost.
Repeated ground patterns such as polygons, circles or stripes, produced by processes including frost sorting and thermal contraction in cold environments.
Weathering, meltwater movement and other processes around persistent snow patches that can help enlarge shallow hollows.

An extensive cover of angular rock blocks, often found on cold upland plateaus. Frost action can contribute to its development, but the blocks may record a long history of weathering. Their presence alone does not prove that permafrost exists today.

The ground above permafrost that thaws in summer and freezes again in winter. Its thickness changes with local climate, vegetation and soil. Seasonal thaw of this layer does not necessarily mean that the underlying permafrost has disappeared.
Ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ice but need not be permanently ice-filled.

misconception.claim: Permafrost is simply a glacier buried beneath the soil.
misconception.truth: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below zero degrees Celsius for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ground ice, but it need not be entirely frozen water. Seasonal thaw can affect the active layer above it, while glaciers are separate bodies of accumulated, flowing ice.

misconceptions.claim: Permafrost is simply a glacier buried beneath the soil.
misconceptions.truth: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below zero degrees Celsius for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ground ice, but it need not be entirely frozen water. Seasonal thaw can affect the active layer above it, while glaciers are separate bodies of accumulated, flowing ice.

teacher.script:
Define permafrost and explain how ground ice differs from a glacier. Play one year and watch the active layer thaw down to the dashed line.

pitfalls: Distinguish processes in cold ground from erosion and deposition by moving glacier ice.
Explain ice wedges through repeated cracking and freezing rather than describing them as river channels.
Consider whether a landform records past cold conditions when interpreting relict features in the Cairngorms.

modelNotes: Permafrost is ground at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years.
The section is 10 m wide and 5 m deep at a common geometric scale.
It assumes permafrost lies beneath an active layer that thaws to a maximum depth of 0.7 m each summer.

labs.title: Storm surge
labs.hook: Onshore winds push water towards the coast, while lower atmospheric pressure also raises the water surface.
labs.objective: Explain how strong winds and low atmospheric pressure can raise coastal water levels, especially over a shallow shelf.
curriculum: Edexcel GCSE A Topic 2 Weather hazards and climate change
Edexcel GCSE B Topic 1 Hazardous Earth
OCR GCSE A Environmental threats to our planet

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Set Onshore wind and Pressure drop to zero and find the reference sea level (dashed line). Raise Onshore wind, then compare two values of Shelf depth.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Onshore wind to zero and Pressure drop to 3000 Pa to see the pressure effect alone. Then combine both, and switch to Physical scale (1:1) to see how small the rise is beside the shelf.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can the same onshore wind produce a larger rise in water level over a shallower shelf?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A wave from a seafloor earthquake
Water piled up by wind and low pressure
A wave from a coastal landslide
questions.explain: Onshore winds can push seawater towards a coast, and low atmospheric pressure can also raise sea level. Shallow shelves and coastal geometry can amplify the resulting storm surge.
Rapid displacement of a large volume of water generates a tsunami, often following vertical seafloor motion. Storm surge instead develops through atmospheric forcing by winds and pressure.

questions.prompt: If you raise Onshore wind, the water should…
choices: Pile up higher towards the coast
Rise evenly across the whole shelf
questions.explain: Stronger onshore wind applies greater stress to the water surface and drives more water towards the coast. In the model, the resulting setup also depends on shelf depth.

questions.prompt: The 1953 North Sea flood and Hurricane Katrina are paired because…
choices: Both were surges from wind and low pressure
Both were caused by river floods
Both were caused by spring tides alone
questions.explain: Both events involved storm winds and low pressure raising coastal water levels over shallow margins. Their different storm types and coastlines affected the timing, extent and severity of the flooding.

why: Onshore winds push water towards the coast, while lower atmospheric pressure also raises the water surface. Shallow shelves can produce a larger setup for the same forcing.
Set Onshore wind to zero and Pressure drop to 3000 Pa to see the pressure effect alone. Then combine both, and switch to Physical scale (1:1) to see how small the rise is beside the shelf.
This steady shelf experiment excludes tides, waves and inundation, which are needed to assess a real coastal flood.

glossary.def: A rise in sea level above the expected tide, driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Coastal shape and water depth influence its size. Surge combines with tides and waves to determine coastal water levels and flooding.

A rise in water level where persistent wind pushes water towards a shore. It contributes to storm surge, particularly over shallow shelves and within bays. Its size depends on wind, duration, depth and coastal shape.

The tendency for sea level to rise where atmospheric pressure falls, and fall where pressure rises. A rough equilibrium estimate is about 1 cm per hectopascal. Storm surge also depends strongly on winds and coastal geometry.

The shallow, gently sloping submerged edge of a continent, extending towards a steeper continental slope. Shelf depth and shape influence tides, waves and storm surge. A shallow shelf can support greater wind-driven water-level rise for the same forcing.

A series of long waves generated by rapid displacement of water, most commonly during a large undersea earthquake. In shallow water they slow and can grow in height. Tsunamis are not caused by the normal daily tides.
Flooding described by the water level after short-period surface waves are averaged out. Coastal still-water level can include the tide and storm surge.
An elongated sandy island lying roughly parallel to the coast, separated from the mainland by a lagoon or other shallow water.

misconception.claim: A hurricane’s wind category fully describes its coastal flood threat.
misconception.truth: Coastal water rise also depends on storm size, track, duration, atmospheric pressure and the shape and depth of the coast. Tide, waves and river flow further affect flooding. A wind category therefore cannot specify the water level or inundation at a particular location.
